## Current Approaches to Scientific Workflows

- Custom Scripts and Domain-Specific Pipelines: Traditionally, scientists implemented analyses with custom scripts (in Python, R, Bash, etc.) or ad hoc pipelines tailored to their domain. This requires significant computational expertise and manual management of data and intermediate results [1]. To lower the barrier, user-friendly workflow platforms like Galaxy and KNIME introduced graphical interfaces for composing analysis steps, while tools like Taverna and Kepler provided domain-specific pipeline frameworks in fields such as bioinformatics. These approaches democratized workflow creation by allowing researchers to build pipelines without heavy programming [2], but the resulting workflows were often tied to specific environments or lacked standardization.

- DAG-based Workflow Engines: Modern workflow management systems treat scientific analyses as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) of tasks. General-purpose engines (e.g., Apache Airflow, Luigi) and science-focused workflow management systems (e.g., Pegasus, Nextflow) automate the orchestration of tasks by managing dependencies, data dependencies, and parallel execution on clusters or the cloud [3]. These systems act as middleware, abstracting away low-level scheduling and data movement, and some provide features like provenance tracking and error handling [4]. The rise of such workflow systems has greatly enhanced scalability and reproducibility in data-intensive fields, prompting the development of community standards for sharing process models and results [5]. Recent workflow tooling also emphasizes pragmatic orchestration and scaling patterns (e.g., minimalist distributed engines, container/job managers, and HPC-oriented workflow layers) [28][29][30][31][32].

- Protocol Registries and Methodological Standards: For experimental workflows (especially behavioral, wet lab, or clinical), researchers often rely on textual protocols and community registries. Detailed step-by-step methods may be published via platforms like protocols.io or as supplementary materials in manuscripts [6]. To improve consistency, domain guidelines have emerged: for example, the CONSORT checklist provides a minimum set of items to report in randomized trial protocols to ensure clarity and transparency [7], and STARD defines standards for reporting diagnostic accuracy studies to enhance completeness and bias assessment [8]. Quality-improvement reporting guidelines such as SQUIRE similarly aim to improve completeness and transparency for complex real-world processes, but they do not provide a machine-checkable process representation [33][34]. In cognitive sciences, data format standards like BIDS (Brain Imaging Data Structure) or Psych-DS prescribe an organization for experimental data and metadata, promoting sharing and reproducibility through a consistent, machine-readable structure [9]. These registries and standards underscore the need for structured workflow documentation, although they focus on reporting and data formatting rather than execution or simulation.

- Workflow DSLs (CWL, WDL, Nextflow): Several domain-specific languages for scientific workflows have gained prominence. The Common Workflow Language (CWL) was designed by the bioinformatics community to encode analysis pipelines in a hardware-agnostic, standardized way, prioritizing portability and reproducibility (at the expense of verbosity and rigid syntax) [10]. In contrast, the Workflow Description Language (WDL) aims for a more human-readable scripting style, offering a gentler learning curve albeit with somewhat restricted expressiveness [11][12]. Nextflow provides its own Groovy-based DSL integrated with a powerful execution engine; it is one of the most mature workflow engines, combining compact, flexible pipeline code with features like portability across environments and built-in provenance tracking [13]. These workflow languages and their runtimes have become dominant in areas like genomics and data science, and enable complex analyses to be defined declaratively and executed reproducibly across compute platforms.

- Emerging Workflow Tools: New approaches continue to push the envelope of workflow usability and reproducibility. For example, Viash automatically wraps analysis scripts into modular, containerized components, complete with standardized command-line interfaces and metadata, so they can plug into larger pipelines [14]. Such components can be directly exported as Nextflow modules, streamlining the integration of custom code into reproducible workflows. Domain-focused frameworks like excitingtools (for materials science simulations) enable automation of complex, multi-step computations and serve as building blocks for high-throughput studies[15]. By providing parsers, data structures, and integration points with workflow managers, these tools address the need for handling intricate domain logic in a systematic way. Likewise, platforms such as DARE (Delivering Agile Research Excellence) offer Workflows-as-a-Service by supporting standard languages (CWL, Python via dispel4py) on cloud infrastructure, with features like on-demand HPC environments and provenance logging for every run [16][17]. Complementary tooling also targets lifecycle capture (e.g., data life-cycle “capsules”) and execution monitoring GUIs for large experiment campaigns [35][36]. These innovations show a trend toward greater modularity, cloud readiness, and automated provenance in scientific workflows.

## Limitations of Current Practices

Despite the progress in workflow engines and languages, current tools have notable shortcomings in modeling complete scientific experiments:

- Limited Readability and Transparency: Many workflow representations remain opaque to those without specific technical training. A pipeline defined in code or YAML (as in Nextflow or CWL) can be difficult for a biologist or clinician to parse, and even experienced users find that complex scripts lack the clarity of a diagram. While languages like WDL were introduced to improve human-readability of workflows[11], in practice even these require understanding of software patterns and jargon. In everyday practice, scientists still resort to textual descriptions and simple flowcharts in papers to describe protocols [6], which can be ambiguous or omit critical details. Even when diagrams are used, comprehension depends on notational choices and layout: empirical work suggests that factors such as scrolling and diagram layout can measurably affect understandability [37][38]. This gap between the machine-readable workflow and the human-readable explanation can hinder reproducibility and multi-disciplinary collaboration.

- Lack of Formal Structure in Protocols: Outside the realm of computational pipelines, there is often no formal, unifying structure to describe an experimental procedure. Experimental protocols are written in lab notebooks or narrative form, leading to siloed, local representations of essentially similar processes[18]. Such free-form documentation makes it hard to compare, reuse, or verify procedures across studies. The introduction of reporting guidelines like CONSORT and STARD underscores that without a structured approach, critical methodological details might be reported inconsistently [7][8]. However, these checklists enforce structure only at the publication stage. During experiment planning and execution, scientists lack a standardized, formal way to represent the workflow itself, which means protocols can remain underspecified or interpreted differently by each researcher.

- Insufficient Traceability: Workflow systems excel at tracking computational provenance (which software produced which output data) but often do not capture the full experimental context. For example, if sample collection or instrument calibration steps are described outside the digital workflow (e.g., manual annotations by humans as in ICA labeling in brain imaging preprocessing), linking those to the analysis results is non-trivial. This fragmented provenance makes it harder to trace results back to every experimental decision. Some newer platforms have started to integrate provenance tracking as a first-class feature (e.g., DARE logs detailed execution traces for later inspection [17]), yet a comprehensive end-to-end traceability -- from study design through execution to data analysis -- is rarely achieved in a single system. Studies on workflow reuse also suggest that simply storing workflows and provenance is insufficient without additional context, annotations, and human-facing visualization to support understanding and reuse [39]. This gap poses challenges for reproducibility, as future researchers may not have a complete map of how inputs (materials, subjects, parameters) were transformed into outputs.

- Poor Alignment Across Stakeholders: Scientific workflows involve diverse stakeholders (experimentalists, data analysts, collaborators, funding agencies, reviewers, etc.) each with different expertise. Current tools do not provide a representation that is equally accessible to all these parties. A detailed workflow specification (code or XML) is aimed at execution engines and developers, whereas other stakeholders prefer high-level visuals or natural language. This misalignment means there isn't a single "source of truth" workflow representation that everyone can refer to. In complex domains like healthcare, it has been noted that lack of a common language for processes impedes communication, and that an ideal modeling language would be "complex enough to incorporate all necessary aspects while being simple enough to be used by non-experts" [19]. The absence of an intuitive yet formal workflow model can lead to misunderstandings, errors in protocol implementation, and difficulty in onboarding new team members to a project's methodology.

## BPMN-Based Modeling for Scientific Experiments

A simple BPMN diagram illustrates an experimental workflow as a series of tasks (rectangle nodes), events (circle nodes), and data objects connected by directed flows. Such BPMN-style diagrams make it easy to visualize the sequence of steps and decision points in a study. The visual clarity helps humans interpret the protocol, while the diagram's underlying formalism allows machines to parse and execute it. Adopting the Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) for scientific workflows offers a promising path to mitigate these issues. BPMN is a widely-used graphical language for business processes, and it can be extended into the scientific domain. Systematic analyses of BPMN extensions and domain applications highlight both the breadth of extension practice and recurring gaps (e.g., domain semantics, methodological guidance, and implementation support), motivating carefully scoped, schema-backed domain profiles for scientific use cases [40][41]. Key advantages of a BPMN-based model include:

- Graphical Clarity: BPMN diagrams use intuitive symbols (e.g. events as circles, tasks as rectangles, gateways as diamonds) to depict the flow of a process. Complex experimental protocols can be presented as flowchart-like schemas that are far more readable than pages of text or code. This visual format aids communication and understanding: stakeholders can quickly grasp the experimental design or protocol logic at a high level. In fields like clinical care, visual process models have been shown to facilitate a "shared understanding" of workflows [21]. By applying similar visual clarity to research workflows, BPMN models make protocols transparent and reviewable by collaborators, auditors, or students who may not be familiar with the underlying code. Best-practice analyses in BPMN-heavy domains (e.g., healthcare) further emphasize the importance of modeling conventions and guidelines to preserve readability and avoid misinterpretation at scale [42].

- Formal Execution Semantics: A critical strength of BPMN is that its diagrams are not just pictures -- they carry formal semantics defined by the BPMN 2.0 standard. This means a BPMN-modeled experiment can be unambiguously interpreted by software. Each step in the diagram has a well-defined behavior (e.g., tasks that trigger execution of certain functions, gateways that implement branching logic, events that handle timers or messages), enabling the workflow to be executed or simulated on a custom or BPMN-compatible engine. In the scientific context, this bridges the gap between documentation and automation: the same diagram that explains the protocol to humans can also serve as an executable workflow specification [22]. The formal underpinning reduces ambiguity (there is less room for misinterpretation of what happens next in a protocol) and ensures that all necessary details (inputs, outputs, decision criteria) are explicitly represented. Ultimately, this improves reproducibility, since anyone running the BPMN workflow (or inspecting its machine-readable form) will follow the exact same steps and logic as the original experiment. Recent work on BPMN and simulation integration further supports the feasibility of connecting BPMN models to simulation/execution tooling while surfacing modeling trade-offs and integration challenges [43].

- Extensibility for Domain-Specific Needs: BPMN's modular architecture allows it to be tailored via extensions, making it adaptable to scientific research requirements. Prior work has demonstrated the feasibility of extending BPMN with custom elements and rules in specialized domains. For example, BPMN4CP (Business Process Model and Notation for Clinical Pathways) introduced healthcare-specific constructs into BPMN to better model clinical treatment processes [23]. This extension incorporated care pathway concepts (like clinical interventions and decision criteria) that go beyond standard BPMN, while still leveraging BPMN's core semantics. Similarly, recent research on human--AI teamwork has resulted in a BPMN extension for agent collaboration, addressing aspects like multi-agent decision making and reliability that vanilla BPMN could not represent [24]. These examples show that BPMN can be enriched to cover concepts such as laboratory tasks, experimental materials, or data quality checks. A BPMN-based Studyflow can thus include domain-specific nodes (e.g. "Cognitive Test" or "Instruction") and data artifacts relevant to scientific work (e.g., "Table" or "Database"), all within a consistent notation. The ability to customize BPMN means that scientists don't have to start from scratch with a new workflow language -- they can build on a proven standard and simply extend it to speak the language of their discipline.

- Unified Communication and Stakeholder Alignment: Perhaps most importantly, a BPMN-derived model serves as a single source of truth that aligns all stakeholders. The same Studyflow diagram can communicate the experiment at multiple levels of detail: it is understandable to humans (thanks to the visual format) and simultaneously interpretable by machines (thanks to the formal structure) [22]. This unity is a stark contrast to current practice where protocol documentation and execution scripts are separate. By using one cohesive diagram to represent the entire research process, Studyflow ensures that researchers, collaborators, and even participants are on the same page [25]. For instance, a Studyflow diagram could be included in a publication's methodology section, giving readers a clear overview of the experimental workflow, and that exact diagram could be executed by a workflow runner to reproduce the analysis or data collection steps. This dual nature -- diagram as both documentation and executable workflow -- provides traceability from design to outcome and fosters greater trust in the process. It aligns with the goals of transparency and rigor in science: much like CONSORT diagrams improved the clarity of clinical trial reporting, Studyflow diagrams can make the conduct of an experiment transparent. Moreover, because the BPMN model is standardized and widely used, it can interface with other systems (lab equipment, data repositories, analysis software) through defined semantics. This extensibility and clarity together empower diverse stakeholders (lab scientists, informaticians, statisticians, reviewers, etc.) to collaborate using a common visual language, reducing miscommunication and error. Conversational and LLM-assisted process modeling further suggests a path toward lowering the authoring barrier while keeping BPMN as the interoperable target representation [44].

In summary, BPMN-based workflow modeling (as exemplified by Studyflow) directly addresses many limitations of current scientific workflow tools. It combines the readability of a graphical flowchart with the rigor of a formal language, yielding workflows that are both human-friendly and machine-executable. Such models enhance traceability (every step is explicit and linked to data), enforce formal structure (via BPMN's schema), and improve stakeholder alignment (one diagram serves everyone's needs). By leveraging a widely adopted standard, this approach also benefits from existing BPMN tooling (model editors, validators, engines) and accumulated best practices in process modeling. As scientific experiments grow in complexity and require greater reproducibility, BPMN-based study flows offer a timely solution: a way to design, document, and execute research workflows in a unified, extensible framework that aligns with both scientific and operational demands[26][27]. The adoption of such models could mark a significant step toward more transparent and maintainable scientific experimentation processes, complementing the strengths of current workflow engines with a higher-level, integrative perspective.
